VS

3. Raja Rajendra Narayan Roy Bahadur, the Zaminder of Bhawal Estate, in the beginning of the 20th century, endowed 20 (twenty) Bighas of land, the boundaries being, in the East-West and North permanent concrete (pucca) Demarcation Pillars of the Government, in the south Government Land and the main Dhakeswari Mandir premises, (situated previously) within Dhakeswari Mohal Khatian No. 2168 under Dhaka Sadar Police Station and presently under Police Station Chawkbazar, District-Dhaka, as Debottar property in the name of the Petitioner No. 1. Sree Sree Dhakeswari Mata, and continued seva-puja of the Petitioner No. 1. After demise of Raja Rajendra Narayan Roy, his three sons, namely; 1) Kumar Ranendra Narayan Roy, 2) Romendra Narayan Roy and 3) Rabindra Narayan Roy endowed the said property in the name of the Petitioner No. 1, Sree Sree Dhakeswari Mata vide Registered `Vogartho Kabuliyat' Deed No.1374 dated 4-4-1908.The deed entrusted the property to the Sebayet, Sree Protab Chandra Chakroborty and other Mudis and Servicemen Praja, living in the said 20 (twenty) Bighas land in 3(Three) specific Shaham of land on condition that they would jointly share the duty of daily Seva-puja, Rituals and Services of the Temple. 

 5. It was further stated in the deed that in case of any repair & maintenance of the Temple, the Mudis and Servicemen Proja along with the Sebayet, all would participate jointly and if any of the Mudis and Servicemen Proja fail to perform any of the above-mentioned duties and abide by the conditions, then the Zaminders or their successors may transfer the possession of the endowed property to anyone else, and the Mudis and the Servicemen Proja even the Sebayet cannot object to, who will be able to perform daily puja and Services towards the Deity and abide by the conditions of the said deed and that the Mudi and Servicemen Proja or their successors in interest will not raise any question in any Court of law in future for such transfer. 

 8. By filing supplementary affidavit, the petitioners further state that while the Cadastral Survey (CS) took place, Deity's land measuring an area of 6.45 acres equivalent to 20 (Twenty) Bighas (Approx.) were recorded in the CS khatians No..16790 (Plot No. 37 & 42), 16791 (Plot No. 33), 16791 (w) (Plot No.40), 16792 (Plot No. 38), 16793 (Plot No. 39), 16794, 16795 (Plot No. 30 & 41), 16796 (Plot No. 31, 32, 34, & 35), 16797, 16798, 16799 (Plot No. 31, 32, 34, & 35), 16800 (Plot No. 31, 32, 34, & 35), 16801 (Plot No. 36) and 16802 (Plot No. 43). The land were Butted and Bounded by the then Government with Concrete (Pucca) pillars and the entire 20 Bighas of property including the schedule property were recorded in the name of Sebayet and other Mudis and/or Service men Proja on behalf of the Deity, Petitioner No.1 as the Dhakeswari Mata alias Oshttabhuja Mata alias Gangadavbya Mata alias Purnabhuja Mata alias Dashabhuja Mata etc. 

 14. The Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka appearing in the Rule Nisi, has filed an affidavit in opposition contending, inter alia, are that 2.56 acres of land under CS Plots No. 30 (part) and 41 (full) under Mauza-Shahar Dhaka. PS Lalbag (the schedule property) were acquired by the Government under the Act, 1948 vide LA Case No. 2 of 1952-53 in favour of M/s Momin Motor Works Ltd. which is a public Requiring Body for development of motor vehicle machineries and work shop. After taking possession of the land. the Government handed over the same to the Requiring Body, Momin Motor Works Ltd. on 24th October. 1952. Accordingly, the Gazette was published under section 5(7) of the Act, 1948 on 28-5-1953 (notification on 25-4-1953) and the land had been vested in the Requiring Body free from all encumbrances. Subsequently, the said land was recorded with the name of Requiring Body. In the aforesaid circumstances, after long years no body can raise any question regarding the said acquisition. The Government did not acquire the Debottar Property or Dhakeswari Mata's Property. 

 16. Further, it is stated that the RAJUK declared some properties alongwith Sree Sree Dhakeswari Mandir as antiquity property and accordingly, gazzette was published. .A civil suit bearing No. 48 of 2015 is also pending before the Court of 5th Joint District Judge, Dhaka in connection with the said acquired land. Over and above, the writ petition involves disputed question of facts as to whether the acquired land belonged to the Dhakeswari Mandir. As such, the Rule Nisi is liable to be discharged. 

 17. The Managing Director, M/s Momin Motor Works Ltd. as respondent No.10 has also filed an affidavit in opposition contending, inter cilia, are that Dhakeswari Mondir is a Temple and the Deity therein existing for years within 1.5682 acres of land in City Survey Khatian and it is bounded by the BUET Staff Quarter in the West, Residential Houses of different peoples in the North, in the East BUET Teachers Quarter and in the South M/s Momin Motor Works Ltd. and the Government road. The claimed property appertained to Bhawal Estate is denied and that alleged "Vogartho Kabuliyat" did not convey any title and it does not attract any identifiable land. The Mahanagar Puja Committee does not have any authority to deal with the property of the Deity. The land of the Deity has been recorded in the name of Deity. The case land is in the enjoyment and possession of this answering respondent for more than 70 years exclusively in its own right. Hence, the alleged claim is barred by limitation. 

 18. The respondent No. 10 further states that immediately after partition in 1947, the Dhaka City was undeveloped and that for the purpose of service providing development in the field of motor vehicles and thereby in order to set up a modern motor vehicle workshop by a company, the property was acquired. Thus, the land was acquired for the public purpose. 

 19. CS Plots No. 41 and 30 were recorded in the name of a private person under a Muslim land lord, namely, Nur Box and he had no connection with the Dhakeswari Mandir. It was recorded in his name as nal land and Kacha Bari and the said property never formed the part of Temple. Government acquired plots No.30 (part) and 41 in LA Case No.2 of 1952-53 under the Act, 1948. The acquisition was notified in the gazette which is apparent from Annexure-C to the writ petition and the land vested in the Government. Thereafter, by an agreement the property was transferred to the Requiring Body, namely, M/s Momin Motor Works Ltd. Thus, the said land was recorded in the name of M/s Momin Motor Works Ltd. in all settlement operation and in the circumstances, the writ petition is not maintainable. 

 20. Land under CS Plots No.41 and 30 are beside the Temple separated by road and that Arbitration Case No. 41 of 1963 was filed by the persons interested in compensation and ultimately they took the compensation. Thus, it proves the falsity of claim of the petitioners and that the Sebayets have been misled to file the writ petition knowing fully well that the Deity had no right and title in the property. Further, in the last 70 years, part of acquired land measuring an area of 1.75 acres had again been acquired for the respondent No.12 (BUET) in LA Case No. 8 of 1982-83 and the petitioners never objected to the same. It is further stated that the Workshop building has become dilapidated and the answering respondent wants to reconstruct the same within its land as per law. The acquired land of the respondent No.10 is demarcated surrounded by the wall. 

 21. By filing supplementary affidavit the respondent No.10 further states that the land under LA Case No.2 of 1952-53 belonged to one Gokul Chandra Roy who purchased the same in auction in 1933. Therefore, the petitioners' claim of ownership in the property before acquisition is not tenable. Further, the gazetted acquired land was claimed as endewed by Raja Rajendra Narayan Roy. But no endowment deed was annexed with the writ petition. Only a Kabuliyat was annexed and the Kabuliyat was executed by a particular person, namely, Sree Protab Chadnra Chakroborty who claimed to be the Shebayet of the Deity. There was no Patta and, as such, the unilateral Kabuliyat did not create any settlement or title. 

 23. The respondents No. 16-18 have also filed an affidavit in opposition contending, inter alia, are that the petitioners claimed that Raza Rajendra Naryan Roy, the Zamindr of Bhawal Estate endowed 20 (Twenty) Bighas of land for the Temple. But the writ petitioners did not have any deed of endowment executed by Raza Rajendra Narayan Roy to prove the genuineness of their claim. The writ petitioners again claimed that after the death of Raza Razendra Narayan Roy, his 3 (Three) sons endowed the said property in the name of the petitioner No. 1, but did not explain once the property was endowed by Raza Rajendra Narayan Roy, what was the necessity for further endowment by his 3 (Three) sons. Further, the petitioners annexed "Vogartho Kabuliyat" but did not annex any "Patta". Without any "Patta" the appointment of Protab Chandra Chakroborty as "Sebayet" cannot be proved. The alleged Kabuliyat appears that it was given in favour of Protab Chandra Chakroborty but not in favour of the Deity. The aforesaid Kabuliyat did not convey any title and it does not attract any identifiable land. 

 ii. The property of the Deity were requisitioned and then acquisitioned through LA Case No. 2 of 1952-53 in accordance with sections 3 and 5 of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 (the Act, 1948). But there was no scope to requisition and acquisition of the Deity's property used by the public for the purpose of religious worship in view of 2nd proviso to section 3 of the said Act. As such, the whole acquisition process under LA case No. 2 of 1952-53 was void, ab-initio and thus, the subsequent LA case being No. 8 of 1982-83 was also illegal and void. 

 iii. The Requiring Body of the acquired property was MIs Momin Motor Works Ltd., a private limited company and the property was acquired for its private purpose. As such, the impugned acquisition was done in violation of sections 3 and 5 of the Act, 1948. 

 a. The requisition and acquisition was made in the year 1952-53 and after a long time (about 65 years), it has been challenged in the year 2015. As such, the petitioners are not entitled to get any remedy under writ jurisdiction due to inordinate delay in seeking equitable relief against the action of the respondents. 

 b. The property was acquired from its lawful owner and possessor namely, Gokul Chandra Roy who purchased the same through auction conducted by the Court in a rent suit. As a lawful owner, he raised objection at the time of acquisition considering which the acquisition process was completed and compen-sation was duly paid to him. Therefore, the petitioners have no locus standi to challenge the said acquisition regarding the case land. 

 c. Since the petitioners had no title or possession in the subject property at the relevant time of acquisition and so, the property was not used by the public for the purpose of religious worship. As such, 2nd proviso to section 3 is not applicable and it is a misconceived writ petition. 

 d. At the relevant time there was no motor vehicle workshop in Dhaka City. The property was acquisitioned for the purpose of maintenance of motor vehicles of the city offices, both Government and public towards development of the city and the public at large for the benefit of city dwellers. Accordingly, an agreement was executed between the Government and the Requiring Body who was brought under contractual obligation to use the acquisitioned property for the public interest. As such, it cannot be said that the property was acquisitioned for the private purpose. e. The writ petition involves disputed questions of title and possession of the acquired property in question. The petitioners have not even produced any undisputed papers showing title and possession of the Deity. As such, their claim in the acquired property cannot be adjudicated under the writ jurisdiction. 

 29. In support of contentions of the respondents, learned Advocates refer to the cases of Achyutananda Das vs Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of land and others reported in 13 BLC (AD) 147, Mollah Industrial Estate vs Khawja Md Arifullah and others reported in 61 DLR (AD) 99, Al-Haj Abdul Maleque Gazi vs The Govt of the People's Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner; Chandpur and others reported in 13 MLR (HCD) 184, Abdul Kader and other vs AK Noor Mohammad and others reported in 36 DLR (AD) 261, Abdul Malek vs The Government of the represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Communication, Secretariat Building, Ramna, Dhaka Bangladesh, and others reported in 16 MLR (AD) 440, Abdul Jalil vs Md. A. Samad and others reported in 7 DLR page 29 and the case of Municipal Corporation of the City of Jabalpur vs State of Madhya Pradesh and another reported in AIR 1966 (SC) 837. 

 2. The Deity being a perpetual Minor, can not suffer for the inability of its management/Sebayet in coming to the Court to challenge the impugned acquisition at the earliest opportunity. As such, considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the alleged delay may be condoned in seeking remedy by the Deity. 

 3. The acquisition having been done in clear violation of prevailing law, it was a public wrong and this continuing wrong is an issue under this writ jurisdiction. 

 4. The petitioners do not claim the property by virtue of the Kabuliyat as annexed to the writ petition and the statements made in the writ petition to some extent are not correct. The Kabuliyat has been annexed only to show a reference as to the existence of the Deity in the year 1908. 

 6. At the relevant time of acquisition, the Deity was the owner of the subject property and accordingly, the CS record was prepared with the name of the Deity (Lakheraj Gangadebba). Therefore, the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka had no legal sanction to acquire the Deity's property in view of 2nd proviso to section 3 of the Act, 1948. 

 7. The Articles of Association and the Memorandum of Association of the Momin Motor Works Ltd. (Requiring Body) can only show as to whether it acted for the public purpose or public interest. But in the absence of such documents, it cannot be said that the acquisition was done for public purpose. 

 33. Since 1952 until 2015, the acquisition has not been challenged. In the circumstances, at the very outset question arises whether the petitioners can get any relief in such a belated writ petition filed after about 65 years from the date of impugned Gazette Notification of the acquisition in question. There are a good number of cases through which the principle annunciated by our Apex Court discouraging to entertain judicial review in a belated writ petition. But here the petitioner No.1 is a Deity and the Deity being a perpetual Minor, we are of the view that due to inability of the Management/Sabayet, the Deity should not be deprived of in seeking legal remedy, even under the writ jurisdiction. Hence, it is an exception to the ratio of the Apex Court and so, explanation for the delay is acceptable as because the justice seeker is a Deity, a perpetual Minor. 

 Provided further that no property used by the public for the purpose; of religious worship, grave yard and cremation ground shall be requisitioned: Provided further that when a property is required permanently for public purpose or in public interest, the Deputy Commissioner may also requisition it with a view to its permanent acquisition for such public purpose or in such public interest 

 5. Acquisition of property.—(1) The Government may, if it thinks fit, acquire any requisitioned property on the proposal of the Deputy Commissioner in the manner hereinafter provided in this section. 

 (la) The Deputy Commissioner shall, if he considers that the acquisition of any requisitioned property is expedient for a public purpose or in public interest, cause a public notice to be given at convenient places on or near the requisitioned property stating that the property is proposed to be acquired. …………” 

 35. From the submissions of the contending parties And on a plain reading of the aforesaid provisions, it is palpably clear that the proposed property for requisition and acquisition has to be required for a public purpose or in public interest. Secondly, the property used by the public for the purpose amongst others of religious worship, cannot be requisitioned in view of 2nd proviso to section 3 of the Act, 1948 and thereby cannot be acquired under section 5 of the Act, 1948. 

 37. To address the issue, we have gone through the cited cases referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioners and other materials on record, in particular, an agreement was executed on 24-10-1952 between the then Government and the Requiring Body. In the said agreement, it was specifically stated that in the acquired land an workshop would be established for the purpose of repairing and manufacturing motor vehicles towards development of Commerce and Industries of the then Province. Specific clause written in the agreement runs as follows: 

 "And whereas the Provincial Government being satisfied that the Land in question is needed for the construction of the Workshop to the aforesaid Company which is likely to prove useful to the development of Commerce and Industries of the province, has consented to the requisition of the aforesaid land under the aforesaid Act, without prejudice to the question of acquisition of the land till an enquiry under section 5 of the aforesaid Act is made. 

 39. We have also gone through the case of Radha Kanta banik vs Province of East Pakistan represented by the Secretary, Revenue Department, Govt of East Pakistan and others reported in 22 DLR (SC) 166 cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioners. Here, the Appellate Division held that the requisition and acquisition of the property can not be done for private purpose. In that particular case, there was a Petrol Pump over the land under acquisition and that by way of acquisition it was vested in favour of a private person (requiring Body) and considering this fact, it was disapproved by the said judgment holding as follows:— 

 The fact remains that the impugned requisition and acquisition were made for the business purpose of a private party.  By the impugned orders, the appellant's business of running a petrol pump was requisitioned and thereafter acquired for M/s Ashish Corporation. As an agent of Caltax Oil (Pak) Limited. M/s Ashish Corporation will sell petrol and petroleum products from the requisitioned and acquired petrol pump and earn commission on such sales. Whoever may be the agent in respect of this petrol pump, the consumer will get supply of petrol and petroleum products as usual, and the person holding the petrol pump as an agent will earn commission on the sales thereof. Thus the impugned requisition and acquisition will directly benefit M/s Ashish Corporation, but the facility for supply to the consumers will continue to remain the same.  In this view of the matter, it is plainly clear that the impugned requisition and acquisition for the business purpose of a private party like M/s Ashish Corporation were not for public purpose. nor were these made in the public interest." 

 40. From the aforesaid ratio, we find that the Apex Court disapproved the acquisition given to a Requiring Body, a private company because of the fact that before acquisition it was a Petrol Pump selling fuel to the public and after acquisition it remained Petrol Pump selling fuel to the public. But only the ownership was changed by the acquisition and thereby the benefit was given to a private person. Here in the present case, facts are different inasmuch as by the acquisition, an workshop was established in the year 1952 when motor vehicles repairing facilities were not developed in the Dhaka city and the Government ensured by an agreement to provide this service to the public i.e city dwellers. Therefore, the impugned acquisition for development of Commerce and Industries by setting up a motor workshop to provide service to the city dwellers, is of course, a public purpose being for the interest of the public. As such, the cited case is not applicable in this particular case. Rather we find support from the case reported in 1999 BLD (AD) 87 wherein our Apex Court held as under:— 

 11. Furthermore, it will indeed be unconscionable if after about 22 years the appellant which is a public body be expropriated when it had built buildings on the acquired land upon making all necessary payments to the Government. Again, there is no principles of law under which once a property has been valid] acquired for a public purpose, as admitted by the Government and has vested in the requiring body then even if the said property by utilized for a different purpose, the acquisition shall  not stand void. A simple reading of section 8B of the Act shows that it does not come into operation in the circumstances of the case. So the order of withdrawal from acquisition in question cannot be sustained. 

 44. But disputing this claim, Mr. Garib-e-Newaz, learned Advocate for the respondent No.10 submits that the acquired plots attracted latest Khatian being No. 16795 and it reflects the superior land lord was Nurbox who got it under section 106 and 108(A) of the Bengal Tenancy Act (BT Act) through auction purchase. Nurbox being tenancy holder engaged the Chatradhari Koiry in the land in question under rent for Tk. 40/-. Further, learned Advocate has drawn our attention to the Annexure-1 to the supplementary affidavit filed by the respondents No. 16-18, a sale Certificate of the Civil Decree Suit No. 75 of 1929 corresponding to Suit No. 20 of 2018 by which learned Advocate submits that after CS survey the property was sold in auction in execution of a Court decree against Prahallat Muhant Wary and others and in the execution case one Gokul Chandra Roy became the auction purchaser. He has drawn our attention to the following schedule from the order sheet of Civil Decree suit No. 75 of 1929 which runs as follows:— 

 Seen nemo No.4887- Reqn. nt. 16-4-52 from Addl. Assistant secy. F& Revenue deptt, with request to stay delivery of possession of the land in question to Momin Motor works Ltd. & further requests to submit a report as to whether the land in question belongs to the Dhakeswari Temple authority or there is any objection on religious ground to the requisition acquisition of the land for the establishment of the Momin Motor works.  Stay further proceeding until further order from Govt. My report in this connection is being submitted to LAC as asked for. 

 Seen Govt. memo No. 4931- Reqn. dt. 16-4-52 directing to enquire if there is any objection on religious or any other reasonable ground to the Acquisition of the land in question for the establishment of Motor Work shop there by the Momin Motor work Ltd. Is directed by Govt, & LAC a local enquiry into the matter will be held on 20-4-52 at 9.a.m issue notice upon all the interested parties & put up S.R. to me on 19-4-52 positively. 

 Seen objection petition dated 10-12-52 filed on behalf of Babu Gokul Chandra Roy s/o late Gour Chandra Roy of Delbazar, Farashganj, Dacca raising objection against requisition And  acquisition of C.S. plot No. 30 & 41 of Sheet No.  20, Ward No. VI of Mouza Sahar Dacca, J.L.No. 343. None appears to press for the objection petition although the petitioner was asked for to do so fixing to-day as the date of hearing. 

 However, I have examined the contents of the objection petition carefully. It appears that  objections have been raised amongst others on the  around that the site being contiguous to the  famous Dhakeswari Temples, the establishment of Motor Workshop there would disturb the peace of the temple and wound the religious sentiment of the Hindu Public. Almost similar objection petitions were submitted by the Same petitioner to DM and to Govt. immediately after the site was brought under requisition. The grounds of objections were thoroughly enquired into and after due consideration of all facts these were rejected by both DM and Govt. In the circumstance stated above the present petition does not appear to me worthy to be tenable. Requisition and acquisition of the site in question  is, therefore, recommended. 

 48. From the aforesaid order sheets of the relevant LA Case No. 2 of 1952.53, it appears that in the proposed acquired land ownership of the petitioner Deity had not been reflected in an enquiry and rather Gokul Chandra Roy was found the owner of the schedule property. However, in view of submissions of the learned Advocates for both the parties and the documents as referred to by the contending parties, in particular, the sale certificate issued in the rent execution proceeding by which the schedule property was sold in auction to Gokul Chandra Roy in 1933 and also the order sheets of the relevant LA Case No. 02 of 1952-53 it is reflected that the schedule property was acquired from the auction purchaser Gokul Chandra Roy as the owner of the same. Further, from the order sheet it appears that at the time of acquisition, there was an enquiry considering the fact of existence of a Temple adjacent to the schedule property and it was never raised that the schedule property belonged to the Deity. 

 49. Inspite of above scenerio, since by referring to the CS Khatians learned Advocate for the petitioners claims title of the Deity in the acquired property, we are of the view that the writ petition involves a disputed question of facts to be ascertained as to whether before acquisition, the property belonged to the Deity and used for religious worship. Unless it is settled, we are not inclined to adjudicate the legal issue under this Rule Nisi as to the propriety of acquisition made by the respondent-Government under LA case No. 2 of 1952-53 in accordance with sections 3 and 5 of the Act, 1948. In the circumstances, before challenging the acquisition, the petitioners need to institute a properly framed suit before the competent civil Court of jurisdiction to establish the fact that before acquisition the petitioner Deity had title and possession in the schedule property and that the same was used by the public for the purpose of religious worship. 

 50. In view of above discussions, we hold that the acquisition made in the year 1952 was for public purpose. However, the 2nd proviso to sections 3 and 5 of the Act, 1948 created an embargo to acquire a property used by the public for religious worship. Unless the schedule property belonged to the Deity, applicability of 2nd proviso to section 3 of the Act, 1948 did not arise. Hence, the petitioner Deity has to establish the facts first through a properly framed suit, that the Deity was owner of the schedule property before the acquisition in question and that the property was used by the public for religious worship at the relevant time of acquisition.
